multipleChoice.question: Why is The Enhanced Games presented as turning the usual debate about drugs in sport upside down?
options: It excludes athletes who have previously used banned drugs.
It transfers the testing of sports drugs from competitions to laboratories.
It makes drug enhancement a permitted feature of the competition.
It removes drug restrictions from mainstream professional sport.

multipleChoice.question: Which description best reflects the design of The Enhanced Games?
options: It focuses on three sports and aims to produce world-record performances.
It includes the full Olympic programme and aims to improve drug research.
It centres on team sports and gives participation priority over results.
It is limited to weightlifting and accepts only former Olympic medallists.

multipleChoice.question: Which group of substances is explicitly permitted at the event?
options: Steroids, painkillers and antibiotics
Vitamins, growth hormones and painkillers
Stimulants, antibiotics and vitamins
Steroids, growth hormones and stimulants

multipleChoice.question: Which principle is behind the sports fan's refusal to support the event?
options: Spectators should receive full medical information about every athlete.
Competitors should begin and perform under comparable conditions.
Only regular sports viewers can judge whether competition is fair.
Performance benefits should remain secret until an event has finished.

multipleChoice.question: Why do the organisers compare open drug use with secret drug use elsewhere?
options: To argue that approval and supervision make their approach relatively safer
To suggest that secret users are more likely to break world records
To show that professional competitions already permit the same substances
To claim that medical supervision removes every possible health danger

multipleChoice.question: Which concern best represents the critics' view of the event?
options: Its narrow choice of sports makes its records difficult to compare.
Its drug-approval procedure is too secret for competitors to trust.
It may damage sport's integrity and put participants' health at risk.
Its former Olympians are more interested in money than in competition.

multipleChoice.question: How does the sports fan respond after hearing arguments from both sides?
options: He accepts the event because the drug use is medically supervised.
He becomes uncertain because both sides offer reasonable arguments.
He supports it only if every athlete receives the same drugs.
He remains opposed because unfair competition defeats sport's purpose.

multipleChoice.question: What limitation is implied in the organisers' claim that their approach is safer?
options: It applies only to competitors who have never taken drugs secretly.
It is a comparison with secret use, not a claim that no risk exists.
It depends on all other sporting competitions ending their drug bans.
It concerns athletic performance rather than the way drugs are taken.

multipleChoice.question: How does the idea of "setting a bad example" support the critics' warning about normalising doping?
options: It suggests that imitation could make doping seem increasingly acceptable.
It proves that every spectator will begin taking performance drugs.
It shows that medical staff are responsible for changing sports rules.
It means that former Olympians have already influenced all younger athletes.

multipleChoice.question: What overall conclusion is best supported by the discussion?
options: Official drug approval resolves both the fairness and health objections.
A small range of sports prevents the event from affecting wider attitudes.
Medical controls have not settled the broader controversy over enhanced sport.
Continued criticism shows that secret drug use is the safer alternative.
